summary: Collects the special-purpose IPv6 addresses defined across many other RFCs into one list, such as loopback, unspecified, and documentation ranges. It is meant as a checklist of prefixes that should not be routed on the public Internet, useful when writing filters. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 6890.

eli5.summary: Some phone numbers are for practice or testing only, never real people. This is a list of internet addresses like that, so nobody uses them by mistake.

questions: which ipv6 prefixes should be filtered
subtitle: A checklist of IPv6 address ranges reserved for special purposes that should not appear on the public Internet.

tldr.problem: IPv6 networks need to know which address ranges are reserved for testing, internal use, or special purposes and should not be routed globally.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5156 compiles special-purpose IPv6 address blocks defined across many other RFCs into a single reference list with guidance on how to filter them.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can use this as a checklist when building routing filters and access control lists to keep special-purpose addresses off the public Internet.

today: RFC 5156 is an Informational document that was obsoleted by RFC 6890, which provides an updated list of special-use IPv6 address assignments.

sections.title: Reserved Address Ranges
sections.content:
IPv6 has many address ranges reserved for special purposes: loopback, testing, documentation, private networks, tunneling overlays, and multicast. These addresses must not be routed on the public Internet. Network operators building routers, firewalls, and filtering policies need a definitive checklist of which prefixes to block or handle specially.

RFC 5156 compiles the special-purpose IPv6 addresses defined in other RFCs into one place. It is structured by address type and includes brief guidance on filtering and routing considerations for each block. The document does not define new address ranges; it serves as a reference and checklist.
sections.eli5: Internet addresses come in many flavors. Some are for testing, some for inside a company, some for talking to old computers. This document lists them all so routers know not to send data to them on the Internet.

sections.title: Loopback and Unspecified Addresses
sections.content:
The loopback address ::1/128 is used by a single host to talk to itself, similar to 127.0.0.1 in IPv4. The unspecified address ::/128 serves as a placeholder for any address and must never appear as a source or destination on the Internet.

Link-local unicast addresses (fe80::/10) are only valid on a single link and are used by hosts to communicate with neighbors on the same physical segment before knowing a global address. These three address blocks should never be routed on the public Internet.
sections.eli5: Some addresses are for talking to yourself, some mean "I don't know my address yet," and some only work on your local cable. None of these belong on the Internet.

sections.title: Private and Documentation Ranges
sections.content:
Unique-local addresses (fc00::/7) are like IPv4 private addresses: they are meant for use within organizations and should not appear on the public Internet. Unlike globally routable unicast, unique-local addresses are intentionally not registered with IANA and are only valid within networks that choose to use them.

The documentation prefix (2001:db8::/32) is reserved for use in documentation, examples, and RFCs. Real networks must never use these addresses. IPv4-mapped (::ffff:0:0/96) and IPv4-compatible (::/96) addresses allow communication between IPv4 and IPv6 networks, but IPv4-compatible addresses are deprecated and all three should not appear on the public Internet.
sections.eli5: Some addresses are for companies to use privately, never on the Internet. Some are just for writing examples in books. Old transition tools use special addresses to talk to IPv4, but those don't belong on the Internet either.

sections.title: Transition and Experimental Ranges
sections.content:
6to4 (2002::/16) and Teredo (2001::/32) are transition mechanisms that allow IPv6 traffic to travel through IPv4 networks. These addresses may be advertised when a site is running a 6to4 relay or Teredo tunnel, but they require careful filtering rules to prevent routing loops and security issues.

6bone addresses (5f00::/8 and 3ffe::/16) were used in an early IPv6 testing network and have been returned to IANA. They may be reallocated in the future and should not appear on the public Internet. ORCHID addresses (2001:10::/28) are Overlay Routable Cryptographic Hash IDentifiers used as application-layer identifiers, not for IP routing, so they should not appear on the public Internet.
sections.eli5: Some addresses are for tunneling IPv6 inside IPv4. Some are old experimental ranges that are being reused. One range is for application identifiers, not for sending data. None should route on the public Internet.

sections.title: Multicast and Default Route
sections.content:
Multicast addresses (ff00::/8) are used to send a single message to multiple recipients. The multicast address space includes a scope field to distinguish local, site, and globally-scoped addresses. Only multicast addresses with global scope may appear on the public Internet; multicast routes must never appear in unicast routing tables.

The default route (::/0) represents any IPv6 address and is used only in routing tables to specify the gateway to use for addresses not explicitly matched by other routes. The default route itself is never used as a source or destination address. An IANA Special-Purpose IPv6 Address Registry (100::/64 and similar blocks) allows IANA to allocate ranges for new experiments and special purposes as IPv6 deployment evolves.
sections.eli5: Some addresses send to many computers at once, and only some of those should route on the Internet. The default route is just a recipe for routers: "if you don't know where it goes, send it here." And IANA keeps a drawer for new special-purpose ranges.

sections.title: Practical Filtering Guidance
sections.content:
Network operators should configure routers and firewalls to block or reject traffic using any special-purpose address ranges. Filtering these prefixes prevents accidental routing of internal or test traffic to the public Internet and protects against certain classes of attack.

The security of a network improves when invalid routing prefixes are filtered at network boundaries. Most modern routing hardware allows filtering of these ranges through ACLs (Access Control Lists) or route filters. Implementations should not hard-code these ranges, as IANA may allocate new special-purpose blocks in the future through the Special-Purpose IPv6 Address Registry.
sections.eli5: Build filters in your routers and firewalls to block these addresses from reaching the Internet. It makes your network safer and prevents mistakes from sending secret data where it shouldn't go.

items.label: Loopback
items.desc: Local host communication; does not leave the host.

items.label: Unspecified
items.desc: Placeholder address; must not appear on the Internet.

items.label: IPv4-mapped
items.desc: IPv4 addresses represented in IPv6 notation.

items.label: Link-local unicast
items.desc: Communication on a single physical link only.

items.desc: Private addresses for use within organizations.

items.label: Documentation
items.desc: Reserved for use in documentation and examples.
